title: After Bills, Josh Allen pummel Jets, how close is the AFC East race to being finished?
author: Joe Buscaglia
content:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The New York Jets lost their veteran quarterback at halftime and couldn’t get into the end zone. The Buffalo Bills, behind their MVP candidate quarterback, scored on a pair of 1-yard sneaks and a pair of explosive plays. That was enough for the Bills to pull away from their AFC East rivals in a 31-12 win on Sunday in front of a MetLife Stadium crowd filled with plenty of blue jerseys.

Jets quarterback Geno Smith was injured on a brutal hit just before halftime. Rookie Cade Klubnik made his NFL debut on the first drive after halftime, went back to the bench for New York’s next drive, but then finished the game when Smith exited with an ankle injury.

Bills quarterback Josh Allen, meanwhile, scored on two 1-yard sneaks and also threw for a touchdown. He has now rushed for at least 10 touchdowns in four consecutive seasons.

The Bills (8-1) became the first team to hit eight wins this season, and widened their division lead over the second-place New England Patriots, who fell to 5-5 earlier Sunday.

It was the fifth straight loss for the Jets (2-8). Coach Aaron Glenn, in his second season, remains winless against AFC East opponents, with a 0-10 mark. His three losses to the Bills have come by a total of 66 points.

Box score | Week 10 live coverage | Game discussion

When New England won in Orchard Park six weeks ago, a season-long AFC East battle sounded tantalizing.

Now, it seems like fantasy.

Week 4 remains the Bills’ lone loss. They’re back in command and on their way to reclaiming the division crown the Patriots borrowed last year. Sunday at the Meadowlands, the Bills made the game harder than it had to be, yet dispatched the Jets rather comfortably.

New England, meanwhile, owns five losses already. Buffalo might not lose that many all year.

The Patriots have dropped three of their past four, the one victory over the awful Miami Dolphins. In a blowout loss to the Detroit Lions today in Germany, Patriots quarterback Drake Maye suffered an ankle injury.

Buffalo is the only AFC East team not currently operating with a backup quarterback.

Allen against these randos is unfair. Yes, we can scrutinize Buffalo’s strength of schedule as we did with New England’s a year ago. Buffalo has faced a sequence of Baltimore’s Joe Fagnano (undrafted rookie in his NFL debut), Carson Wentz (so bad that Minnesota traded for Kirk Cousins), Klubnik (fourth-round rookie in his NFL debut) and, next week against Miami, Kyle McCord (sixth-round rookie who made his NFL debut Sunday).

The Bills, though, deserve credit for forcing two of those debuts. Their good fortune hasn’t totally been gifted. Lamar Jackson fractured and dislocated his throwing thumb on edge rusher Greg Rousseau’s pressure. The Bills knocked Smith from Sunday’s game with a crunching combo hit from linebacker Terrel Bernard and edge rusher T.J. Parker.

So the Bills continue to feast and win comfortably. Allen saved the Bills’ defense for two months. Now, the defense is thriving and hasn’t allowed 18 points over the past three games.

The Bills can keep pummeling these overwhelmed quarterbacks like sparring partners, preparing them for the main events ahead. From Thanksgiving to Christmas, the Bills will play the Kansas City Chiefs, the Patriots in Foxboro, the Green Bay Packers in Lambeau Field and the Denver Broncos at Mile High.

Perhaps the Patriots can make up ground if the Bills lose a couple of those difficult matchups, but it’s difficult to envision the Bills giving up four games’ worth of cushion.

The only foreseeable way Buffalo gets caught is if Allen joins the list of AFC East starters knocked out of commission. — Tim Graham, senior writer
,

The Bills offense did its best Jekyll-and-Hyde impression on Sunday between the first and second halves. Although they sustained some drives, the Bills seemed hesitant to try to attack the Jets deep through the air in the first half. The Jets came into the game with the second-worst defensive success rate in the NFL, but the Bills sleepwalked their way through the first half, only averaging 4.3 yards per play and managing only 10 points. It allowed New York to stay in the game for far too long, and the Bills were clearly frustrated as they went into halftime.

Allen and company woke up in a big way in the second half, once they started forcing the issue deep downfield. Predictably, the Jets offered little resistance, starting with the Bills’ first play of the half — a 54-yard strike to tight end Dalton Kincaid. Over their five second-half series before garbage time, the Bills averaged 14.4 yards per play, scored three touchdowns and had four plays of 20 or more yards, three of which went for 40-plus. The three touchdown drives took a combined seven plays. That goes to show the potential of the best offense in the NFL, despite the sleepy start. — Joe Buscaglia, Bills beat writer

The Bills wasted little time giving Hooker, their big trade deadline acquisition, a full workload. After only four full days in the building, Hooker played every snap for the Bills as one of their two starting safeties and shifted former starter Damar Hamlin into a reserve role. Hooker’s impact was immediate. They took away the deep middle of the field and enabled their other starting safety, Cole Bishop, to be used in a versatile and dynamic role as Hooker was patrolling over the top.

Having Hooker on the field was especially important in this contest because the Bills’ four-man pass rush was not getting home as quickly as it had in the early stages of the season, which led to a lot of coverage-based pressure opportunities. With some real injuries to their secondary (cornerback Christian Benford and nickel corner Dee Alford), Hooker becomes that much more important to a secondary that has played much better as of late. — Buscaglia

When Smith was being evaluated for a concussion at the start of the third quarter, Klubnik showed just enough on his first series to whet the appetite of Jets fans. There might’ve been a real quarterback controversy on the Jets’ hands — at least among fans — had that been the end of his afternoon.

Instead, Smith left the game again and the Bills exposed some of Klubnik’s flaws — or at least the downsides of his gunslinger mentality. Klubnik showed on that first drive that he’s unafraid when he completed a 33-yard pass to Garrett Wilson. As the Jets neared the end zone, he took a couple of failed shots, at least one of which was nearly picked off. He also flashed some mobility and a willingness to scramble for yards that doesn’t exist in Smith’s game, gaining 19 yards on two carries.

When Klubnik came back in, he looked a bit wild and out of control on some inaccurate passes on the move — one of them was even picked off only to be fumbled back to the Jets after a big hit by tight end Jeremy Ruckert. That drive still went nowhere after a new set of downs. On his next drive, Klubnik held onto the ball too long two different times and was sacked on both, so the Jets went three-and-out, wasting a rare defensive interception.

Klubnik had New York’s offense moving in the fourth quarter with the game still in hand, but the drive ended in typical Jets fashion — with Wilson making a catch, confusingly trying to lateral it back to Kenyon Sadiq, missing him terribly and fumbling it back to the Bills, who then scored on a 74-yard touchdown run on the ensuing play.

Klubnik’s final stats: 11-of-20 for 137 yards and an interception. — Zack Rosenblatt, Jets beat writer

It would be hard to say Glenn won’t survive this one in particular — few, if anyone, thought the Jets would keep it close with the Bills, especially with the state of the defense and even more so once Smith went down and the Jets were forced to turn to a fourth-round rookie at quarterback.

But that doesn’t excuse the way things went in other ways — the frequency of back-breaking penalties in key moments, like a Malachi Moore defensive pass interference on third down in the first quarter, followed up a few plays later by a defensive holding on Kingsley Enagbare that set up an easy Allen touchdown run. There was the moment in the second half where Glenn had Moore, who had barely played at all until last week, covering wide receiver D.J. Moore one-on-one, which led to an easy touchdown pass. The run defense continues to be confoundingly ineffective, and the pass rush is often invisible. That all plays into the biggest failure for Glenn this season — play calling was supposed to be his “superpower,” and it has never really felt like he’s put the defense in position to succeed.

On the other side of the ball, the Jets had six offensive drives reach Bills territory, and they didn’t score a touchdown in any of them — extending their touchdown-less streak to nine quarters.

At this point, it would be practically impossible for anyone to reasonably believe Glenn has what it takes to turn the Jets season around fast enough to save his job. But by all accounts, he’s expected to stick as the head coach at least through the end of the regular season. — Rosenblatt
